cse-2015-2-cs-13.approach: Check each statement against how cookies actually work: a cookie is a small piece of **data** (name=value plus attributes) set by the server, never executable code.

steps.title: What a cookie is
steps.body: A server sends `Set-Cookie: name=value; Expires=...; Path=...` in the HTTP **response header**; the browser stores the text and returns it in the `Cookie:` request header on later requests to that site. It is plain data — it is never executed.

steps.title: Test each statement
steps.body:
- (A) "a piece of code" — **false**: a cookie is data, so by itself it cannot run or compromise a machine.
- (B) enters via an HTTP header (`Set-Cookie`) — true.
- (C) `Expires` / `Max-Age` give an expiry date and time — true.
- (D) a site can use its cookie (e.g. a session/user id) to track the pages a user visits on it — true.

steps.title: Pick the NOT-correct one
steps.body: Only (A) is incorrect.

answer.value: **(A)** — a cookie is data, not code

optionAnalysis.reason: Incorrect statement (so this is the answer): cookies are passive name=value text, not executable code.
Correct statement: cookies arrive in the `Set-Cookie` HTTP response header.
Correct statement: the `Expires`/`Max-Age` attribute sets the expiry date and time.
Correct statement: a site's cookie identifies the browser on each request, so its browsing pattern on that site can be tracked.

pitfalls: Confusing cookies (data) with scripts or malware; privacy risk from tracking is not the same as code execution.
cse-2015-2-cs-13.verification: Each of B, C, D is a standard RFC 6265 cookie property; only A contradicts the definition of a cookie.

cse-2015-2-cs-15.approach: The recursive call comes **before** `putchar`, so characters print in reverse order while the recursion unwinds; recursion stops at the first space.

scene.caption: Recursion descends to the space and stops.

steps.title: Deepest frame returns
steps.body: `foo(" EFGH")` fails the test and returns at once without printing. Control is back in the frame for `D`, right after its call on line 3.

steps.title: Print while unwinding
steps.body: Each frame prints its own character **after** its child returns: deepest first, so `D`, then `C`, `B`, `A`. Output: `DCBA`.

scene.caption: Frames return D → C → B → A, each printing its character.

Right characters but forward order — that is print-then-recurse.

steps.title: Cost
steps.body: The path length is the height $\lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor$. In the worst case (root is the smallest key) it must sink all the way, so $\Theta(\log n)$ operations are needed: the bound is $\Omega(\log n)$.

cse-2015-2-cs-23.approach: Deadlock is possible only if every process can hold fewer than its maximum while all resources are taken; with max 2 each this needs $N \ge 6$. None of the options reaches that, so the question as printed is flawed; the published key is (D).

steps.title: Deadlock-free condition
steps.body: With $m$ identical resources and each process needing at most $k$, deadlock is impossible when $N(k-1) + 1 \le m$: even if every process holds $k-1$, one resource is left to let some process finish.

steps.title: Apply it
steps.body: Here $k = 2$, $m = 6$: $N(2-1) + 1 \le 6 \Rightarrow N \le 5$. So $N = 1, 2, 3, 4$ are all deadlock-free; the smallest $N$ that could deadlock is $6$ (six processes each holding 1 and waiting for 1).

steps.title: Reading the options
steps.body: No option can deadlock as printed. The commonly published key is (D) $N = 4$, the largest value offered; treat this question as erroneous.

answer.value: As printed none can deadlock (needs $N \ge 6$); published key **(D) 4**

Holding 1 each leaves 4 free — no deadlock.
Holding 1 each leaves 3 free — no deadlock.
Published key; but holding 1 each still leaves 2 free, so strictly this cannot deadlock either.

pitfalls: Using $N \cdot k > m$ (8 > 6) as a deadlock test — that is not sufficient; check $N(k-1) + 1 \le m$.

cse-2015-2-cs-26.approach: Look at the singularity at $x = 0$: $f$ blows up there, but $|x|^{-1/3}$ is integrable because the exponent is less than 1.

steps.title: I and II
steps.body: $f(x) = x^{-1/3}$ is undefined at $x = 0$ and $|f(x)| \to \infty$ as $x \to 0$. So $f$ is **not continuous** on $[-1,1]$ (I false) and **not bounded** (II true).

steps.title: III — area
steps.body: Area $A = \int_{-1}^{1} |x|^{-1/3}\,dx = 2\int_0^1 x^{-1/3}\,dx = 2\left[\tfrac{3}{2}x^{2/3}\right]_0^1 = 2 \cdot \tfrac{3}{2} = 3$. Nonzero and finite: III true.

optionAnalysis.reason: Misses III: the area is 3, finite and nonzero.
Misses II: $f$ is unbounded near 0.
Correct.
I is false: $f$ is not even defined at 0.

pitfalls: Taking the signed integral (0, since $f$ is odd) as the area.
Assuming unbounded ⇒ infinite area.
cse-2015-2-cs-26.verification: Each half contributes $\tfrac{3}{2}$; $p = \tfrac13 < 1$ so $\int_0^1 x^{-p}dx$ converges.

cse-2015-2-cs-28.approach: A self-complementary graph has exactly half of all $\binom n2$ possible edges, so $\binom n2$ must be even.

steps.title: Edge count
steps.body: $G \cong \bar G$ ⇒ $|E| = |\bar E|$ and $|E| + |\bar E| = \binom n2$, so $|E| = \frac{n(n-1)}{4}$ must be an integer.

steps.title: Condition on n
steps.body: $4 \mid n(n-1)$. Since $n$ and $n-1$ have opposite parity, one of them must be divisible by 4: $n \equiv 0$ or $1 \pmod 4$.

steps.title: Examples
steps.body: $n = 4$: path $P_4$; $n = 5$: cycle $C_5$; both self-complementary — so neither "even" nor "odd" nor "multiple of 4" alone is right.

Wrong: $n = 5$ works; $n = 6$ fails ($15$ edges is odd).
Wrong: $P_4$ has $n = 4$; $n = 3$ fails.
Correct: forced by $n(n-1)/4 \in \mathbb Z$.

pitfalls: Picking (A) because $P_4$ is the textbook example and forgetting $C_5$.

steps.body: Right = 25, below = ∞ → move **25** left. The hole at (3,4) has nothing to its right and ∞ below, so it becomes ∞.

steps.body: RFC 1323/7323 limits the shift count to 14, so the largest window is $65535 \times 2^{14}$ bytes (about 1 GB).
